problems.title: The energy identity for the minimum-norm solution

solution.text:
(a) A⁺A is the orthogonal projection onto C(A^T): split x = x_row + x_null with x_row ∈ C(A^T) and x_null ∈ N(A). Then A⁺A x_row = x_row (A⁺ is a right inverse on the row space) and A⁺A x_null = 0, so P = A⁺A is the orthogonal projection onto the row space. The row space has dimension m (A has full row rank with probability one), so P = Σ_{i=1}^m u_i u_i^T for any orthonormal basis {u_i}.
(b) The row space of a Gaussian A is a uniformly random m-dimensional subspace: the distribution of A is invariant under orthogonal transformations, hence so is the row space. Each u_i is therefore uniformly distributed on the unit sphere, and E[u_i u_i^T] is invariant under conjugation by any orthogonal Q, so it must be a scalar multiple of I; taking traces gives the scalar 1/n.
(c) E||Px||² = x^T E[P] x = x^T (Σ_i E[u_i u_i^T]) x = (m/n)||x||². Since the minimum-norm solution is Px, E||x − Px||² = ||x||² − E||Px||² = (1 − m/n)||x||², so the expected relative error is sqrt(1 − m/n).

problems.statement:
### Problem 14-1 — The energy identity for the minimum-norm solution

The minimum-norm solution $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}^{+}\mathbf{b}$ is the projection of the true signal onto the row space of $\mathbf{A}$. This problem derives the expected energy of that projection.

(a) Let $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ be Gaussian with $m < n$. Show that $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{A}^{+}\mathbf{A}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathsf{C}(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf T})$, and write $\mathbf{P} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^{\mathsf T}$ for an orthonormal basis $\{\mathbf{u}_i\}$ of the row space.

(b) By rotational invariance of the Gaussian distribution, show that $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^{\mathsf T}] = \tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{I}$ for each $i$.

(c) Conclude that for any fixed $\mathbf{x}$,

$$
\boxed{\ \mathbb{E}\lVert \mathbf{P}\mathbf{x}\rVert_2^2 = \frac{m}{n}\lVert \mathbf{x}\rVert_2^2\ },
$$

and hence the expected relative error of the minimum-norm solution is $\sqrt{1 - m/n}$.

problems.title: Sparsity of the minimum-ℓ1 solution

solution.text:
(a) With x = x⁺ − x⁻ and x⁺, x⁻ ≥ 0, the constraint Ax = b becomes A x⁺ − A x⁻ = b, and at the optimum the supports of x⁺ and x⁻ are disjoint, so ||x||_1 = 1^T x⁺ + 1^T x⁻. The problem is a standard-form LP with 2n variables and m equality constraints.
(b) The LP has an optimal solution (the objective is bounded below by 0 and the feasible set is nonempty), and standard LP theory guarantees an optimal basic feasible solution, i.e. a vertex of the polytope {z ≥ 0 : Bz = b}. A vertex is determined by m linearly independent active constraints among the 2n nonnegativity constraints, so at most m variables are nonzero.
(c) Hence x = x⁺ − x⁻ has at most m nonzero entries. For a K-sparse signal with m ≥ K measurements the true signal is feasible for the ℓ1 problem and the ℓ1 minimizer is K-sparse (at most m nonzeros), so basis pursuit can in principle recover it; the RIP guarantees that it does.

problems.statement:
### Problem 14-2 — Sparsity of the minimum-$\ell_1$ solution

Basis pursuit minimizes $\lVert \mathbf{x}\rVert_1$ over the affine set $\{\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\}$. This problem shows that the solution is sparse.

(a) Let $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ have full row rank. Write the problem as a standard-form linear program in the variables $\mathbf{x}^{+}, \mathbf{x}^{-} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}^{+} - \mathbf{x}^{-}$ and $\mathbf{x}^{+}, \mathbf{x}^{-} \ge 0$:

$$
\min_{\mathbf{x}^{+}, \mathbf{x}^{-}} \ \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}^{+} + \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}^{-}
\quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}^{+} - \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}^{-} = \mathbf{b}, \quad \mathbf{x}^{+}, \mathbf{x}^{-} \ge 0.
$$

(b) Argue that the optimum is attained at a vertex of the feasible polytope, and that a vertex has at most $m$ nonzero coordinates. (A basic feasible solution of a standard-form LP with $m$ equality constraints has at most $m$ nonzero variables.)

(c) Conclude that the minimum-$\ell_1$ solution has at most $m$ nonzero entries. Why does this make basis pursuit a plausible recovery rule for $K$-sparse signals with $m \ge K$ measurements?
